title: How to Pay Employees With Multiple Pay Rates (+ Overtime)
summary: Paying employees with multiple pay rates? Learn how to track hours by role, meet minimum wage, and calculate blended overtime, with two examples.
body_markdown:
Student Agencies, a student-run nonprofit at Cornell, has more than 300 people in its system and runs 50 to 70 of them through any given payroll. People join for a month, switch roles, and pick up new wages along the way. "It is really helpful to have that feature be where you can add in employees, add them in different roles, constantly change their roles, change their wages," says Riley McGuire, the group's Director of HR.


You don't need 300 people to run into the same need. A cashier covers three shift-lead closes. A server picks up host shifts on slow nights. Paying employees with multiple pay rates is legal and common, but it adds three things to get right: tracking hours by role, keeping every rate at or above minimum wage, and calculating overtime when the rates differ.


This guide covers the five steps, both federal overtime methods with the math worked out, the rules for tipped roles, and the mistakes that lead to back pay.


## Quick Answer: How to Pay an Employee Two Different Pay Rates


1. **Record hours by role.** "42 hours" isn't enough. You need "30 hours as a cashier, 12 as a shift lead."
2. **Pay each hour at that role's rate.** Every rate has to meet the minimum wage for that job and location.
3. **Add up hours across all roles.** Overtime starts after 40 total hours in the workweek, not 40 per role.
4. **Use the weighted average for overtime by default.** Divide total straight-time pay by total hours, then pay an extra half of that rate for each overtime hour.
5. **Or agree on the rate in effect ahead of time.** With a written agreement made before the work, you can pay 1.5 times the rate of the job worked during the overtime hours.

## Can You Pay an Employee Two Different Hourly Rates?


Yes. The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) lets you pay one employee different hourly rates for different kinds of work. The only floor is that every rate has to be at least the minimum wage that applies to that job. Put each rate in writing when you hire someone or add a new role to their plate.


Common reasons one person ends up with more than one rate:


- **Different roles.** Server and host, cashier and shift lead, barista and trainer.
- **Shift differentials.**[Extra pay for nights, weekends, or holidays](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/shift-differential) .
- **Departments or locations.** The same person works the kitchen at one store and the front at another.
- **Temporary assignments.** A higher rate for covering a manager's shifts or running inventory.


## How to Pay Employees With Multiple Pay Rates in 5 Steps


### Step 1: Set a Bona Fide Rate for Each Role


Give every role[its own hourly rate](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/what-is-pay-rate) and write it down. Federal rules call this a "bona fide" rate: it meets the minimum wage for that work, and it's the rate you pay for that job during regular, non-overtime hours (29 CFR 778.419). You can't invent a low rate that only shows up when overtime does.


### Step 2: Track Hours by Role at Every Clock-In


A timecard that says "42 hours" doesn't tell you what to pay. You need hours split by role, including shifts where someone switches jobs halfway through. The easiest way is to have people pick their role when they clock in.


That's how Student Agencies handles a team that's always changing. "It kind of made sense that we could just add them on Homebase, have them clock in and clock out and we wouldn't need to worry about manually tracking everybody," Riley says.


> In Homebase, each team member can have multiple roles, each with its own wage, so hours are tagged by role from the moment someone clocks in.[See how the time clock works.](https://www.joinhomebase.com/time-clock)


### Step 3: Calculate Straight-Time Pay for Each Role


Multiply the hours in each role by that role's rate, then add the totals together. This is the employee's straight-time pay for the week, and it's the starting point for any overtime math.


### Step 4: Add Up All Hours and Check for Overtime


Overtime is based on[total hours worked for you in the workweek](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/overtime-on-biweekly-payroll) , not hours per role. Someone who works 30 hours as a cashier and 15 as a shift lead has five overtime hours, even though neither role hit 40. A few states, including California, also require daily overtime, so check your state's rules too.


If you run payroll every two weeks, line up your workweek with your pay period so overtime never splits across two paychecks. "To stay compliant with the weekly overtime reset rule, biweekly employers should make sure the start day of their workweek matches the start day of their pay period. If your pay period is biweekly and runs Monday through Sunday, your workweek should also run Monday through Sunday," says Cambria Wallace, Project Lead II, Payroll Operations at Homebase.


### Step 5: Calculate Overtime and Review Before Payday


Use one of the two methods in the next section, then show every rate and its hours on the[pay stub](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/free-pay-stub-template) so the employee can follow the math. Before you submit, scan for anything that looks off. Riley compares each person's hours by role against the last pay period: "If someone worked like 10 hours the last pay period and suddenly is working like 50 hours, that's something to be alarmed by and go back and check."


## How Do You Calculate Overtime With Multiple Pay Rates?


Under federal law, you have two options. The default is the weighted average method: divide total straight-time pay by total hours to get a blended regular rate, then pay half that rate for each overtime hour. The alternative pays 1.5 times the rate of the job being worked during overtime, but only with an agreement made before the work.


Overtime rarely shows up on schedule. At The Hidden Garden, a florist, last-minute orders change the week fast. "Someone needs something, and it causes everyone to go into two hours of overtime or three hours of overtime," says owner Amy Marella. When those hours land on someone with two rates, here's how to pay them.


### Method 1: The Weighted Average (Blended) Overtime Rate


This is the default under[29 CFR 778.115](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-B/part-778/subpart-B/subject-group-ECFR7be43dce58760d9/section-778.115) . The formula:


- **Blended regular rate** = total straight-time pay ÷ total hours worked
- **Overtime premium** = blended rate × 0.5 × overtime hours
- **Total pay** = straight-time pay + overtime premium


**Example:** Jordan works 30 hours as a cashier at $18 and 15 hours as a shift lead at $22 in one workweek.


1. Straight-time pay: (30 × $18) + (15 × $22) = $540 + $330 = **$870**
2. Blended regular rate: $870 ÷ 45 hours = **$19.33 an hour**
3. Overtime premium: 5 hours × ($19.33 × 0.5) = **$48.33**
4. Total pay: $870 + $48.33 = **$918.33**


Why only half the rate for overtime? The $870 already pays Jordan straight time for all 45 hours, including the five overtime hours. The premium adds the missing "half" to make those hours time and a half.


### Method 2: The Rate-in-Effect Method (Advance Agreement Required)


Under[29 CFR 778.419](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-B/part-778/subpart-E/subject-group-ECFRa03ba49ecef2bc3/section-778.419) , you can pay overtime at 1.5 times the rate of whichever job the employee is doing during the overtime hours. Four conditions apply:


- The employee does two or more kinds of work.
- Each job has a bona fide hourly rate.
- You and the employee agree to this method before the work is done. Put it in writing.
- Overtime is paid at no less than 1.5 times the rate for that job.


**Example:** Same week for Jordan. The result depends on which job pushed them past 40 hours.


- **If the last five hours were shift-lead hours:** (30 × $18) + (10 × $22) + (5 × $22 × 1.5) = $540 + $220 + $165 = **$925**
- **If the last five hours were cashier hours:** (25 × $18) + (15 × $22) + (5 × $18 × 1.5) = $450 + $330 + $135 = **$915**


This method needs precise timestamps so you know exactly when someone crossed 40 hours. You also can't switch methods week to week to pay whichever comes out lower.

## Tipped Roles and Minimum Wage: The Dual-Jobs Rule


If one of an employee's roles is tipped, the[tip credit](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/tipped-minimum-wage-by-state) only applies to hours in that tipped job. Hours in a separate non-tipped job, like prep cook or dishwasher, need at least the full minimum wage. Federally, that means $2.13 an hour in cash wages is allowed for server hours (with tips covering the rest of the $7.25 minimum), but not for prep hours. Some states, including California, don't allow a tip credit at all.


> **Recent change (October 2026):** The federal "80/20 rule," which limited how much side work a tipped employee could do, was struck down in court in 2024. On October 19, 2026, the Department of Labor[withdrew the last opinion letters](https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/whd/whd20261019-0) behind it and said a new proposed rule on tipped employees is coming. Check for updates before setting policy.


Tipped roles also change the overtime math. When you calculate the regular rate, count tipped hours at the full minimum wage, not the $2.13 cash wage ([29 CFR 531.60](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-531/subpart-D/section-531.60) ). For example, in a state that follows the federal minimum and allows a tip credit,[like Texas](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/texas-minimum-wage) , a server who works 30 tipped hours and 15 hours as a host at $10 has a regular rate of ($217.50 + $150) ÷ 45 = $8.17 an hour, and five overtime hours add a premium of $20.42.


## State Rules That Change Multiple Pay Rate Math


Federal rules set the floor. Your state can add to it:


- **Higher minimum wages.** Many states and cities set minimum wages above $7.25, which raises the floor for every rate you pay. Check your[state labor law guide](https://www.joinhomebase.com/state-labor-laws) .
- **Daily overtime.** California requires overtime after eight hours in a day and[double time](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/calculating-double-time-pay) after 12, on top of the weekly rule.
- **Which method you can use.** California's Labor Commissioner uses the weighted average method. In *Levanoff v. Dragas* (2021), a state appeals court allowed the rate-in-effect method because it paid employees more overall, so don't assume it's safe if it would pay less.


## Common Mistakes When Paying Multiple Pay Rates


Most multi-rate payroll errors come from a few predictable places:


- **Paying 1.5 times the blended rate on top of straight time.** This counts the straight-time half twice. In Jordan's example, it would pay $1,015 instead of $918.33. The[Texas Workforce Commission](https://efte.twc.texas.gov/i_employees_two_rates.html) calls this out as a common error.
- **Counting overtime per role.** Overtime is based on total weekly hours, so 30 hours plus 15 hours is five hours of overtime.
- **Defaulting to the highest rate.** Paying overtime at the higher rate is allowed, but it's a choice to pay more, not a rule. For Jordan, it would cost $1,035.
- **Using the rate in effect without an agreement.** If you didn't agree on it in writing before the work, the weighted average applies.
- **Taking a tip credit on non-tipped hours.** Prep, dish, or host hours need the full minimum wage.
- **Not tagging hours by role.** Without it, payroll turns into guesswork, and so does finding the source of high overtime. Before The Hidden Garden had a clear breakdown, figuring out why overtime ran high took "hours! I would do a search each night and morning to see where we were and why," Amy says.


Most of these come down to the same habit. "To prevent calculation errors with hourly employees working overtime across multiple pay rates or locations, use company timesheets, and keep up with time cards daily so you're not caught off guard by hours worked and overtime amounts on payroll day," Cambria says.


## Is Overtime Taxed Differently With Multiple Pay Rates?


Starting with 2026 Forms W-2, employers have to report employees' qualified overtime pay in Box 12 using code TT. That's the amount employees can use for the[federal overtime deduction](https://www.joinhomebase.com/blog/is-overtime-taxed-more) . Qualified overtime is the extra pay above the regular rate required by the FLSA, so for someone with two rates, the blended-rate math directly sets the number you report. Only the FLSA-required half-time counts, so California daily overtime or double time above the federal requirement isn't reported as qualified overtime. Getting the overtime calculation right now saves you from filing a Form W-2c later. See the[IRS overtime deduction FAQs (FS-2026-13)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/taxpros/fs-2026-13.pdf) for details, and talk to your tax professional about your situation.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Multiple Pay Rates


### Can an Employer Pay an Employee Two Different Rates?


Yes. Federal law allows different hourly rates for different kinds of work, as long as every rate meets the minimum wage that applies to that job and location. Document each rate in writing, track hours by role, and include all of the rates when you calculate overtime for the week.


### Is Overtime Calculated at the Higher Rate?


Not by default. Federal rules use the weighted average of all the rates worked that week. You can pay 1.5 times the rate for the job worked during overtime hours only if you and the employee agreed before the work. Paying the highest rate is allowed, but it costs more than the law requires.


### What Is a Blended Overtime Rate?


A blended overtime rate is the weighted average of every rate an employee earned in a workweek. Divide total straight-time pay by total hours worked to get it. For each overtime hour, add half of that rate, because straight-time pay for those hours is already included in the total.


### How Do You Calculate Weighted Average Overtime?


Multiply hours by rate for each role and add the totals. Divide by total hours to get the regular rate. Multiply the regular rate by 0.5, then by the overtime hours, and add that to straight-time pay. For example, $870 ÷ 45 hours = $19.33, and five overtime hours add $48.33.


### Does Overtime Apply if Each Role Is Under 40 Hours?


Yes. Overtime is based on total hours worked for the same employer in a workweek, not hours per role. An employee who works 30 hours as a cashier and 15 hours as a shift lead has five overtime hours, even though neither role went past 40 on its own.


### How Do You Pay a Server Who Also Works as a Host?


Track server and host hours separately. Pay the tipped cash wage only for server hours, where your state allows a tip credit, and at least the full minimum wage for host hours. When you calculate overtime, count server hours at the full minimum wage, not the lower cash wage.


### What Payroll Service Handles Multiple Pay Rates?


Look for a payroll tool that stores several roles and wages for each employee, captures the role at clock-in, and moves hours into payroll without re-entry. Homebase does this for hourly teams, and so do larger providers like ADP, Gusto, and QuickBooks. Ask any provider how it calculates multi-rate overtime before you switch.


## Pay Every Role Right, Every Week


Multiple pay rates come down to three habits. Track hours by role, keep every rate at or above minimum wage, and remember that the overtime premium on a blended rate is half-time, not time and a half on top of everything.
